tagline: A former logging tunnel carries cars into Kentucky’s sandstone gorge
intro: The Red River Gorge Scenic Byway travels through a landscape of stone arches, caves, cliffs and ravines. The Federal Highway Administration lists this National Scenic Byway at 46 miles and allows one hour for driving or five for exploring, emphasizing its scenery, natural features and recreation. Within the Daniel Boone National Forest, the gorge’s geological area contains more than 100 natural sandstone arches. The gorge also contains rock shelters and waterfalls among its high sandstone cliffs.

One passage into that landscape began as a timber route. Dana Lumber Company had Nada Tunnel cut through solid sandstone; narrow-gauge locomotives hauled logs through it to a Clay City sawmill. After the forests were cleared and the companies left, workers removed the rails and laid a dirt road for horses and pedestrians. Pavement followed, but the tunnel carries only one lane of road traffic.

Enter the gorge through Nada Tunnel on Kentucky Route 77. Later in the journey, Slade provides a base for climbers visiting the gorge. Two miles south of Slade, Natural Bridge State Resort Park lies beside the geological area. Its sandstone arch spans 78 feet and rises 65 feet, a final change from a passage cut by people to one formed by weathering.

moments.title: Nada Tunnel
moments.text: The first trainload of logs got stuck. Nada Tunnel had been cut only 12 feet high and 12 feet wide; blasting freed the load, and the tunnel was made a foot taller. Two teams had worked from opposite sides of the ridge, using dynamite, steam machinery and hand tools to remove the sandstone. The resulting 900-foot passage through solid sandstone on Kentucky Route 77 outlasted its railway use. After logging ended, the rails gave way to a dirt road for horses and pedestrians, followed by pavement for a single lane of cars.

moments.title: Slade
moments.text: Slade serves as a lodging base for Red River Gorge climbers. Its connection with climbing reached the screen in the 2004 documentary Red River Ruckus, which featured the community and a local campground. The community is also home to Natural Bridge State Resort Park.

moments.title: Natural Bridge
moments.text: Natural Bridge’s Original Trail dates from the 1890s, when the Lexington and Eastern Railroad developed this place as a tourist attraction. The half-mile trail leads to a sandstone arch spanning 78 feet and standing 65 feet high. Railroad ownership changed in 1910 when the Louisville and Nashville bought the Lexington and Eastern. In 1926, L&N president Wible L. Mapother transferred the property to the Kentucky State Park Commission. The park’s trails cross uneven terrain with moderate to strenuous difficulty. Beneath the arch, a narrow rock passage carries the name Fat Man’s Squeeze.
moments.notice: The sandstone arch spans 78 feet and stands 65 feet high.
